t: Count Paths With the Given XOR Value — Bitwise-State Grid DP
o: Count monotone (right/down) lattice paths from corner to corner whose XOR of cell values equals k (< 16). Example 1 has three such paths. Since cell values and k are below 16, XOR states live in [0, 16), so we carry a DP table of size n x 16: dp[j][x] = number of paths reaching column j of the current row with XOR x. Transitions OR-in arrivals from the left and from above, XORed with the current cell's value. Complexity O(m*n*16) — trivial for a 300x300 grid.
k: Small value domain (grid values, k < 16) means the XOR can be an explicit DP dimension with only 16 states.

a.n: Approach 1: Row-Rolling DP over XOR States
a.i: Process cells in row-major order with a rolling array indexed by column. When computing cell (i, j), dp[j] still holds row i-1's values (the cell above) and dp[j-1] holds the current row's processed value (the cell to the left) — exactly the two predecessors needed. Each predecessor's count at XOR x flows to XOR x ^ grid[i][j].
s: For each cell (i, j) except the start, build cur[x ^ v] += dp[j-1][x] (if j > 0) plus dp[j][x] (if i > 0).
a.t: O(m*n*16) — each cell relaxes 16 XOR states from at most two predecessors.
a.sp: O(n*16) — one rolling row of state vectors.

w: Whenever a path statistic ranges over a tiny domain (here 4-bit XOR), make it a DP dimension — the same trick handles AND/OR/sum-mod-small-M. Pitfalls: updating dp in place incorrectly (compute cur fresh per cell so the 'above' values are not yet overwritten), and forgetting the modulo on accumulation. Edge cases: 1x1 grids (answer is grid[0][0] == k), and k unreachable (returns 0 naturally). Follow-up: k up to 1e9 with values < 16 (state space unchanged — XOR of small values stays small), or counting paths with XOR at least k.
